blocks.text: The poem’s own frame matters: Isaiah 14:4 identifies it as a taunt against the king of Babylon. The “day-star, son of the morning” language belongs within that poem of a ruler’s proud ascent and humiliating fall. Identifying this figure with Satan belongs to later Jewish and especially Christian reception; it is not the poem’s explicit addressee.

Isaiah’s wider collection addresses Judah, Israel, and foreign nations, portraying empires as accountable for their actions even when they function within the book’s larger portrayal of history. That setting helps place this chapter’s judgments on Babylon, Assyria, and Philistia within a broader concern for the nations as well as Israel.
